claims.text: In single-phase HEAs, solid-solution strengthening caused by lattice distortion is the primary mechanism governing hardness and strength.
Compositional complexity induces lattice distortion in HEAs.
Greater lattice distortion inhibits dislocation movement.
Inhibition of dislocation movement by lattice distortion increases hardness and yield strength.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can produce a uniform, equiatomic, single-phase HEA without secondary phases.
Controlled thermal annealing can adjust lattice distortion while grain size and composition remain constant.
Small changes in constituent-element atomic-size mismatch can systematically alter lattice distortion.
Annealing substantially below the recrystallization temperature avoids grain growth and phase transformation.
Atomic-size mismatch generates local strain fields in the crystal lattice.
Local strain fields increase resistance to plastic deformation by impeding dislocation motion.
HEAs with greater measured lattice distortion will have higher hardness than a lower-distortion baseline.
HEAs with greater measured lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than a lower-distortion baseline.
Less aggressive annealing conditions can provide a lower-lattice-distortion baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to alloys that remain single-phase and lack significant contributions from secondary phases or grain-boundary strengthening.
The proposed relationship applies under room-temperature quasi-static loading.
Annealing can modify lattice distortion without causing significant recovery or recrystallization.
The magnitude of strengthening may depend on atomic-size differences, interactions among alloying elements, and residual microstructural variation.
X-ray diffraction line broadening or high-resolution electron microscopy can quantitatively measure the relevant lattice distortion.
A lack of statistically significant correlation between measured lattice distortion and both hardness and yield strength would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome associates lower distortion with less aggressive annealing, whereas the falsification design proposes minimizing distortion through a strain-relief heat treatment. The implied direction of the annealing effect is inconsistent or insufficiently defined.

The boundary requires annealing to alter lattice distortion without significant recovery, while the low-distortion condition is produced by heat treatment that promotes strain relief, which ordinarily invokes recovery-like relaxation. The distinction between intrinsic chemical lattice distortion and recoverable processing strain is not resolved.
